before.approach: Start at the Hoh Ranger Station/Hoh Rain Forest trailhead (578 ft) inside Olympic National Park and follow the Hoh River Trail east. The first 10.5 miles to Lewis Meadows (1,005 ft) are gentle, shaded old-growth rainforest walking along the braided, glacially-fed Hoh River, with numerous log/stream crossings and abundant water the whole way. Continue past the Olympus Guard Station (~9 mi) and cross the High Hoh Bridge (a dramatic span hundreds of feet above the gorge, ~13.2 mi) into steeper, more exposed terrain. Reach Elk Lake (2,500 ft) around mile 15, where the trail begins climbing in earnest toward Glacier Meadows (4,200-4,300 ft, ~17.2-17.5 mi), the standard base camp. In early season expect several steep, consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows requiring an ice axe and crampons. About 0.25 mile before Glacier Meadows the trail crosses a washout/slide area via a roughly 100 ft ladder (sometimes called the Jemrod Gully ladder) supplemented by a fixed rope; this is the crux of the hike-in for many parties. From Glacier Meadows, follow the climbers' way trail about 0.8 mile up onto the crest of the lateral moraine (a narrow, exposed 'catwalk' with loose rock underfoot), then along the moraine crest roughly 0.2 mile before descending onto the toe of the Blue Glacier itself (watch for rockfall on this descent). No camping is permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier. From the glacier's edge it is roughly 4-6 more miles and about 3,700 ft of gain, roped up for crevasse travel, up to Snow Dome (~6,600 ft) and the upper mountain; a notable hazard en route is a large crevasse near Crystal Pass that is often 'impassable' except via a snow bridge that must be scouted each season. July-September is the best window for a straightforward glacier crossing.

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows
approach_variants.notes:
Hoh Rain Forest trailhead (about 578 ft) inside Olympic National Park. The Hoh River Trail runs east; the first ten and a half miles to Lewis Meadows are gentle old-growth walking beside the braided river, with water the whole way. Past the Olympus Guard Station the High Hoh Bridge crosses the gorge and the ground steepens. Elk Lake sits around mile 15 at 2,500 ft, and the trail then climbs in earnest to Glacier Meadows at 4,200-4,300 ft, about mile 17.2-17.5, which is the standard base camp.

About a quarter mile below Glacier Meadows the trail crosses a washout on a ladder of roughly 100 ft with a fixed rope beside it. For many parties that is the hardest part of the walk in.

In early season there are several steep, consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows that want an axe and crampons.

A wilderness permit is required year-round for every overnight stay in Olympic National Park, obtained in advance through Recreation.gov or a Wilderness Information Center, and the Hoh is one of the areas that runs on a daily quota. Camping is not permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier.
hazards: roughly 100 ft ladder plus fixed rope at the washout below Glacier Meadows
steep consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows in early season
narrow, loose lateral moraine crest with rockfall on the descent to the glacier toe
no camping permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant ends at camp, not at climbing. The confirmation you are at Glacier Meadows rather than somewhere short of it is the washout ladder and fixed rope just below it — if you have not climbed a ladder, you are still below.

From the meadows a way trail runs about 0.8 mile up onto the crest of the lateral moraine, a narrow exposed catwalk with loose rock underfoot, then follows the crest roughly another 0.2 mile before dropping onto the toe of the Blue Glacier. The drop onto the ice is where you rope up; nothing before it is glacier travel.

approach_variants.name: Glacier Meadows to the summit block via Snow Dome and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Rope up at the toe of the Blue Glacier and travel up to Snow Dome around 6,600-6,800 ft. This is roped crevasse travel throughout. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is often passable only on a snow bridge, and that bridge has to be scouted afresh each season.

Olympic National Park points climbers at the Crystal Pass line as the standard: from Snow Dome over Crystal Pass, then traversing immediately south of and below Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit, and finally onto the true summit block of the West Peak. It is longer than the alternatives and generally regarded as the safer option through most of the season.
hazards: crevasses throughout - a large crevasse near Crystal Pass often crossable only on a snow bridge that must be scouted each season
bergschrund or moat immediately below the summit block, variable through the season
loose deteriorating scree on the block and on the pinnacle east of it - rockfall onto your own party
the true summit is hidden from the north, so navigation is to a point you cannot see
the false summit is east of the true summit and catches parties out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The only technical climbing on this route is the summit block of the West Peak, and finding it is the crux of the day, because THE TRUE SUMMIT IS NOT VISIBLE from the north side. A party that keeps navigating toward the highest thing it can see from Snow Dome ends up at the five-fingered false summit, which is EAST of where it wants to be.

The rule that works: go south-southeast through one of the two gaps to the LEFT, or far left, of the five fingers, and come at the summit from the east or southeast — approaching an objective you cannot yet see.

Once through, a rising traverse leads to a loose rocky gully; you go up that, over, and down into a second rocky gully, then up a final steep snow slope that delivers you to the foot of the block.

You are there when you are standing under a discrete rock tower roughly 80 ft high. The standard finish is class 4 on loose rocky ramps; there is also a line of about 80 ft straight up the north face on mostly solid rock, around 5.4. If you are under a snow slope with no rock tower above it, you have not arrived — keep going.

Expect a bergschrund or moat immediately below the block. Its state changes through the season and it can force a short detour or a stretch of short-roping; on the pinnacle just east of the West Peak parties have found a schrund below it and deteriorating scree above, and have grouped tightly or moved one at a time because of the rockfall.

before.beta: The West Ridge route approaches from the southern side of the mountain, ascending a series of seven pitches along the broad ridge crest. Snow slopes and ice climbing dominate with Class 5.4 rock scrambles on the final pitches to the summit block. This route is less frequently done than the Blue Glacier standard but offers excellent alpine climbing and less crevasse hazard.

before.grade: Grade III; Class 4 with a Class 5 step
gear: Rope, harness, crampons, ice axe for the Blue Glacier approach and Snow Dome
1-2 ice screws for crevasse-rescue anchors — this is a standard glacier walk, not steep ice, so a full crevasse kit is overkill

before.detailed_rack: The summit block requires a small rack of 6-10 cams in sizes ranging from 0.4 to 1.5 inches (or equivalent). Include 2-3 quickdraws, multiple slings (60 cm and 120 cm), and lockers for anchor building. The East Face ramps are often ascended with minimal protection due to poor rock quality; protection is intermittent and bomber placements are rare. Bring 2-3 ice screws (10 cm length) for ice/névé anchors on Snow Dome. Rappel anchors typically use natural rock features or pre-existing slings, but climbers should build solid anchors as backups.

pro_tips: Start summit day in pre-dawn darkness (3-4 AM) to minimize rockfall exposure on the East Face and avoid afternoon thunderstorms
Carry a 60-meter rope late season (July-August onward) to avoid multiple rappel stations; 40-50m may require intermediate anchors and extra time
Use a small, lightweight alpine rack (6-10 cams, slings, quickdraws); most teams climb the summit block with minimal gear and good footwork
The Snow Dome is a broad, gently sloping platform; in whiteout conditions, use a GPS waypoint or compass bearing to navigate toward Crystal Pass to avoid wandering
Acclimatize at Glacier Meadows for at least one full day before summit attempt; the 4,200-7,980 ft push in a single day is taxing
Bring extra layers and a windproof shell; the summit is severely exposed and weather can change in minutes

before.rappels: 1 rappel of 25-30 m down the northwest edge to a belay ledge, then scramble and downclimb to rejoin the standard East Face ramps descent. The 30 m low end of this route's own gear note is enough to CLIMB the single pitch but reaches only 15 m doubled, and a 50 m reaches 25 m with nothing spare.

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome to the base of the summit block
approach_variants.notes: Identical to the standard approach for every route on this peak: Hoh River Trail from the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center about 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows at roughly 4,300 ft, the moraine way path and the drop onto the Blue Glacier, roped glacier travel across the flat lower ice and up through the rock islands right of the icefall to Snow Dome at about 6,600-6,800 ft, then Crystal Pass, the traverse below Five Fingers Ridge, the false summit, and the sharp saddle beneath the true summit pyramid. The only thing this route changes is what you do once you are standing at the foot of the tower.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug; early or late season this face can carry ice, which changes it from a 5.4 pitch into something else
hazards: Fixed tat at the top of the pitch is old and unmaintained — inspect and back it up
The face is steeper and more exposed than either other summit-block finish, and holds ice early and late in the season
The descent rappel measures close to a full 165 ft, which eats nearly all of a 60 m rope doubled with nothing to spare
Everything on the approach: Blue Glacier crevasses, the Crystal Pass crevasse, moraine rockfall, whiteout on Snow Dome
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SHARED ARRIVAL TEST IS THE FLAT SNOW TOP AT THE FOOT OF THE 80 FT TOWER, on its northeast side, where the steep snow slope out of the saddle stops rising.

THE TEST THAT YOU ARE ON THIS FINISH AND NOT ONE OF THE OTHER TWO IS ROPE, NOT ROCK, AND IT IS THE BEST FOG MARKER ON THIS MOUNTAIN. Enough parties end up on this exact line that a semi-permanent rappel station has built up at the TOP of it — a boulder or horn wrapped in slings with a rap ring and a quick link. From the platform, look straight up the face above you. If there is tat hanging down the line you are about to climb, that is the North Face Direct and you are in the right place. If there is no tat above you, you are looking at the east-face ramps (round the corner to the right) or the northwest edge (round to the left), and you have not found this finish.

The fixed gear is not agency-maintained and slings weather fast, so back it up and do not lower onto it unexamined — but as a piece of route-finding evidence in cloud it is unambiguous, because it is the only fixed anchor on the block and it hangs down THIS face.

SECOND TEST: the pitch is a single rope length of about 165 ft on generally solid rock at 5.4, steeper and more exposed than the ramps. If your first fifty feet is a wandering scramble across ledges rather than a face, you have drifted onto the ramp system.
